newsitem.title: USA: NYS Comptroller gives mixed review of welfare plan.
newsitem.headline: NYS Comptroller gives mixed review of welfare plan.

text.p: New York State Comptroller H. Carl McCall said Wednesday that while some aspects of Gov. George Pataki's new welfare plan, were "sound," others, like childcare, and especially jobs, did not go nearly far enough.

Saying New York ranked 49th in the nation last year in creating jobs, McCall, in prepared remarks, said, "Adding tens of thousands of former welfare recipients to that mix without a job creation strategy is a recipe for a nightmare."
"He (Pataki) has not presented any detailed long-term economic development strategy," McCall added.
The workfare aspect of Pataki's new welfare plan, called "NY Works," also was questioned by the Civil Service Employees Association, which represents 265,000 state, municipal and private employees.

"CSEA remains concerned, however, about the potential displacement and inequity of placing increasing numbers of welfare recipients in public sector workfare jobs," the union said, in prepared remarks. Stanley Hornak, a union spokesman said such jobs included entry level and cleaning positions.

Though McCall praised several aspects of Pataki's including letting welfare recipients keep more of what they earn, using a $450 million windfall on public aid, and maintaining full benefits for the disabled. But McCall added Pataki still was not planning to spend enough on childcare.
The stand on childcare that was taken by the comptroller, who is regarded as a potential Democratic challenger for governor, was echoed by an advocacy group.

The New York State Child Care Coordinating Council said, "While closer scrutiny of the Pataki Administration's proposal is needed, the New York State Child Care Coordinating Council is concerned that NY Works won't work because it won't create the hundreds of thousands of additional child care slots families will need in order to work," in prepared remarks.

The Assembly blocked the governor's attempt to reform the state welfare system this spring, and Pataki's new proposal contains a number of the same provisions. The Assembly Speaker, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, is not expected to return from a vacation trip to China until next week, and his staff declined to comment in his absence.
Legislative sources have said that while the Assembly likely is prepared to accept changes mandated by the new federal rules, it probably would fight stricter curbs, like the benefit cuts.
Senate Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, in prepared remarks, said, "Our goals should be to end the cycle of dependency, increase personal responsibility and make the system more efficient."
The governor reiterated that while his goal was to get his welfare bill approved in December or January, the decision hinges on how the legislature reacts.
"I'm going to wait and see the reaction of the legislative leaders. I don't want to call a session to simply have people point fingers or yell," he told reporters in Albany.
New York City sources have speculated that any special session likely would only extend the city income tax surcharge and give lawmakers a pay hike.

New York City, which has 66 percent of the state's welfare caseload, is particularly vulnerable under the new federal rules. City Hall officials, who were not immediately available to comment, had fretted that the state would be tempted to use some of the windfall to close its long-term budget gaps, but Pataki instead has vowed to use the $450 million for social services.

The governor said that his staff has been consulting with the Giuliani Administration on a regular basis, saying "They're very positive." A spokeswoman for Mayor Rudolph Giuliani had no comment immediately available.
